segments: rm, cp, and mv form the basic file-operation toolkit. The following commands fill out the rest of the tools you are likely to use every day.
Viewing and browsing
ls — list directory contents
The most frequently used command, hands down.
A useful mnemonic: ls -lah = see everything + make it readable.
Using wildcards with ls
Creating and deleting
mkdir — create directories
-p is the most frequently used option: it creates missing parent directories automatically and does not report an error if they already exist.
touch — create empty files / update modification times
rmdir — remove empty directories
In practice, rm -rf is more commonly used to remove nonempty directories, but it requires extra care.

Links
ln — create hard links and symbolic links
In everyday use, you will almost always use symbolic links:

A symbolic link is similar to a shortcut, but it stores a path. Deleting the target path breaks the symbolic link. A hard link still refers to the same inode; the file's data is released only after the last hard link is deleted and no process has the file open. Hard links generally cannot cross filesystem boundaries and generally cannot link to directories.
Archiving and compression
tar — create archives
Remember: c = create an archive, x = extract an archive, z = gzip, v = verbose output, and f = specify the filename.
zip / unzip — cross-platform compression
